analysis.one_liner: Opens federal offshore waters and public lands to oil and gas drilling while extending clean energy tax credits.
analysis.headline: The bill won 141 cosponsors from both parties but never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Written during the 2008 gasoline price spike, the bill would have ended long-standing bans on offshore oil and gas leasing along the outer Continental Shelf and on oil shale leasing on federal land, while keeping new drilling at least 25 miles from any state's coast and letting coastal states veto drilling between 25 and 50 miles out [S2][S3]. It would have split the resulting royalties: 30% to the federal treasury, 30% to coastal states, and the rest to conservation, environmental restoration, renewable energy, and carbon capture accounts, with 2% to low-income energy bill assistance [S3]. It also extended a long list of tax credits for wind, solar, efficient appliances, efficient homes, and biofuels, created a new plug-in hybrid vehicle credit, funded clean energy research, and swapped light crude from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve for heavy crude, dedicating the proceeds to weatherization, low-income energy assistance, and energy research [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain access to offshore and oil shale areas long closed to leasing. Coastal states would gain a permanent royalty stream earmarked for education, transportation, and coastal restoration. Renewable energy and biofuel producers, appliance and home builders, and buyers of efficient and plug-in vehicles would gain extended tax credits. Low-income households would gain dedicated weatherization and heating-bill assistance funding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas firms, coastal states, clean energy

how_it_helps.text: It lifts every federal prohibition on offshore and oil shale leasing, including the presidential withdrawals of outer Continental Shelf waters, opening new areas to oil and gas production [S2][S3].
It puts new protections in statute: no drilling within 25 miles of a state's coast, and states can veto drilling between 25 and 50 miles out by enacting a disapproval law within one year [S2][S3].

It dedicates fixed shares of new drilling royalties to conservation, Great Lakes and Chesapeake Bay restoration, renewable energy research, and carbon capture, and gives coastal states 30% of the revenue [S3].
It extends tax credits for wind, solar, geothermal, biomass, biodiesel, energy-efficient appliances and homes, and creates a credit of up to roughly $6,000 for plug-in hybrid vehicles [S3].

It funds roughly $1 billion in programs from a Strategic Petroleum Reserve exchange, including $100 million for low-income weatherization, $100 million for low-income home energy assistance, and research on wind, solar, geothermal, batteries, and carbon capture [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the main cost would be borne by coastal communities and ocean-dependent businesses exposed to new offshore drilling, and by taxpayers through forgone revenue on the extended tax credits. Federal forests would lose protection from biomass harvesting rules, and the federal fleet would lose its requirement that alternative fuels it buys cut lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions compared with conventional fuel.

drawbacks.text: The bill revokes all presidential withdrawals of outer Continental Shelf waters from drilling, so protections would depend on the new 25-mile statutory buffer, which is narrower than the bans it replaces [S2][S3].

It repeals the 2007 requirement that federal agencies only buy alternative or synthetic fuels whose lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions are no higher than conventional fuel's, removing an emissions safeguard [S2][S3].
It allows woody biomass from federal forest lands to count as renewable fuel, raising concerns about harvest pressure on national forests [S2][S3].
New offshore drilling takes years to bring oil to market, so the leasing opening would not deliver quick relief at the gas pump even as it raised spill risk off coasts that currently have none.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a deliberate trade: significant new oil and gas development, especially offshore, exchanged for a 25-mile coastal buffer, state veto rights, a dedicated royalty stream for conservation and clean energy, and a large package of efficiency and renewable tax credits. For coastal states and ocean-dependent businesses, the trade looks worse than for inland or energy-consuming households, and the repeal of the synthetic-fuel emissions rule is a genuine loss. On balance the bill mixed real help for energy bills and clean energy with a major expansion of fossil fuel extraction.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to seven House committees in July 2008 and to three subcommittees in the fall, but none of them ever took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2009 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. John Peterson of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on July 31, 2008, at the height of that summer's gasoline price debate, and it drew 141 cosponsors, 41 Democrats and 100 Republicans [S1][S4].
The House referred it to seven committees at once: Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Science and Technology, Education and Labor, Budget, and Rules [S1][S5].

Its only further movement was referral to subcommittees on Energy and Air Quality, Energy and Mineral Resources, and Energy and Environment between August and September 2008; no committee ever held a markup or reported it to the floor [S5].
Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill was never voted on in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of expanded offshore drilling kept the existing moratoria in place, since the bill died without a vote. At the same time, nothing in its renewable tax credits, weatherization, or low-income energy assistance became law through this bill either, so supporters of those programs gained nothing here. The record simply shows a bipartisan compromise that never moved past subcommittee referral [S1][S5].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of offshore drilling kept status quo

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship split across both parties from the start: 41 of 233 House Democrats and 100 of 201 House Republicans cosponsored [S4].

industries.note: The bill's core would open offshore waters and oil shale lands to leasing and permanently entrench drilling as the funding source for conservation and energy programs. Coastal states and beach- and ocean-dependent businesses would bear the spill and industrialization risk, while consumers would see new supply only after long lead times.
Multi-year extensions of production and investment tax credits for wind, solar, geothermal, and biodiesel, plus new royalty-funded renewable energy reserves, would directly support the industry.
Extended credits for efficient appliances, homes, commercial buildings, and a new plug-in hybrid vehicle credit would create customer demand for these products.

Opening outer Continental Shelf waters to leasing near state coasts would expose beaches and fishing grounds to drilling infrastructure and spill risk, a cost this bill asks coastal industries to carry.
